data.title: Adamas Trust 3Q 2026: Revenue $194.5M, Net loss $171M, EPS $(1.89) — 10-Q Summary
data.description:
Adamas Trust reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $194.5M, down 0.9% from the prior-year quarter, and a $171M net loss attributable to common stockholders, compared with net income of $32.7M a year earlier. Diluted loss per share was $(1.89), versus earnings per share of $0.36.

Financial Highlights

  • Revenue was $194.5M, compared with $196.3M in the prior-year quarter; YoY change (0.9%).
  • Net loss attributable to common stockholders was $171.0M, compared with net income of $32.7M in the prior-year quarter.
  • Diluted EPS was $(1.89), compared with $0.36 in the prior-year quarter.

Business Highlights

  • Adamas acquired $1.2B of Agency investments and approximately $394.5M of residential loans, including $390.1M in business-purpose loans.
  • Its Constructive platform funded $376.5M of business-purpose loans, and management said it intends to continue scaling the platform.
  • Late in the quarter, the company added TBA short positions to reduce Agency exposure amid rising rates. It reduced those positions by approximately $2.6B after quarter-end.
  • The company completed a rental-loan securitization and a non-Agency RMBS re-securitization to support portfolio financing.
  • Management expects market volatility to persist and plans disciplined portfolio growth and prudent capital allocation focused on recurring income.

data.title: Midterm US elections, earnings, jobs data loom for AI-wary stock market
data.description:
Key points:
  • Investors eye possible Democratic win in Congress, potential AI impact from vote
  • Apple, AMD, Palantir among Q3 reports due in coming week
  • Monthly jobs report on Friday comes after Fed holds rates steady

By Lewis Krauskopf

US midterm elections, a heavy slate of corporate earnings and the monthly jobs report will further test stock investors next week, after a series of setbacks for the market-leading AI trade.

The latest AI turbulence stemmed from disappointing quarterly results of Alphabet and Amazon , two hyperscalers spending massively on data centers, while shares of semiconductor company Intel tumbled nearly 29% on Friday following its report.

Dragged down by tech and AI-related stocks, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX sank 1.8% on Friday while the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.9%.

The quarterly results intensified concerns about financing and financial returns needed to support the AI investment theme at the heart of the US bull stock market. The questions are likely to persist, with Apple , AMD and Palantir among the major tech and AI players due to report next week. Also, the midterm elections could determine the outlook for AI regulation.

The stock market "seems a bit troubled to me, and I think that really stems from the AI fears that seem to be persistent, if not building," said Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at retirement and wealth services provider Empower. "There is still some digestion around what we saw with earnings this week."

MIDTERM VOTE COULD AFFECT AI

Tuesday's elections will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. Democrats are widely predicted to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is more in doubt. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of the Trump administration.

Investors are bracing for increasing pushback on data centers, whose impact on energy costs and the environment has led to intense public opposition. Despite doubts that any viable legislation will pose serious risks to AI investment, regardless of which party wins, a Democratic sweep is expected to bring more scrutiny. Investors are also watching local and state races in Texas and elsewhere on Tuesday for their implications for the data-center buildout.

"To the extent that the Democrats really do have a significant blue wave, I think that will be seen as negative for both the AI names, for tech to some extent in general, and maybe even for the market as a whole," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments.

Defense and healthcare are other stock market areas that could be sensitive to the election results. Any shift in Washington could affect the outlook for fiscal spending that could reverberate through asset prices. A Democratic sweep could bring more regulatory scrutiny, including for Wall Street banks and crypto firms.

ALSO ON TAP: APPLE, AMD RESULTS, JOBS DATA

Robust earnings performance has underpinned equity gains so far in 2026. With over half of the S&P 500 having reported third-quarter results, overall earnings were on pace to rise 31.6% for the period, according to LSEG IBES data on Friday.

Investors were punishing some reports. For example, Caterpillar shares sank 9% on Thursday after the company stuck to its annual sales growth forecast despite strong demand for its power equipment from data centers.

"The earnings bar is very high," said Chris Galipeau, head market strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute. "And if you miss or don't jump over that bar, you're in trouble."

Apple reports on Monday, with the iPhone maker's shares up about 27% so far this year. Results are also expected from semiconductor companies AMD and Qualcomm as well as Palantir, which offers another view of the AI trade. McDonald's , Amgen and ConocoPhillips are among over 100 S&P 500 companies that are due to report next week.

Next Friday's employment report for October will give a critical read into the health of the US economy.

Data on Thursday showed the US economy in the third quarter grew at its fastest pace in a year, as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI. The Federal Reserve this week upgraded its assessment of the economy as it held interest rates steady.

"I think the missing piece of this strong economic growth narrative is the lack of job growth," said Matthew Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments.

Other areas of the market have picked up the slack as AI and related technology stocks have struggled. For October, the energy and financial sectors posted solid monthly gains, as did defensive groups such as utilities and healthcare. The S&P 500 was last up over 10% on the year.

"The market is much more broad than people generally want to give it credit for," Galipeau said.

data.title: Richmond Mutual reports Q3 net income of $1.75 million
data.description:
Richmond Mutual reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $1.75 million, or diluted earnings per share of $0.11, compared with $2.23 million in the prior quarter and $3.60 million a year earlier. Results included a $6.12 million provision for credit losses and $3.0 million in merger-related expenses, partly offset by a preliminary $1.6 million bargain purchase gain. Net income for the first nine months of 2026 was $6.76 million, or $0.56 per diluted share.

Financial Highlights

  • Net interest income was $22.85 million, up from $12.07 million in the second quarter and $11.30 million in the third quarter of 2025.
  • The provision for credit losses was $6.12 million, compared with $823,000 in the prior quarter and $269,000 a year earlier. Net charge-offs totaled $6.1 million during the quarter.
  • Noninterest income was $4.56 million, including a preliminary $1.6 million bargain purchase gain. Noninterest expense was $20.01 million and included $3.0 million in nonrecurring merger-related expenses.
  • Net income was $1.75 million, or $0.11 per diluted share, versus $2.23 million and $0.22 per diluted share in the second quarter of 2026 and $3.60 million and $0.36 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.
  • For the nine months ended September 30, net income was $6.76 million, or $0.56 per diluted share, compared with $8.17 million, or $0.82 per diluted share, in the same period of 2025.

Business Highlights

  • Richmond Mutual completed its merger with Farmers Bancorp on July 1, 2026. The Farmers Bank subsequently merged into First Bank Richmond.
  • The combined bank operates as First Bank Midwest. The holding company remains headquartered in Richmond, Indiana, and the bank is headquartered in Frankfort, Indiana.
  • The combined organization had 24 full-service offices at September 30, 2026, serving communities in Indiana and Ohio.
  • The bank elected to report regulatory capital status under the Community Bank Leverage Ratio framework effective September 30, 2026.

data.title: Stocks fall on AI cash burn worries while bonds rally with oil
data.description:
Key points:
  • Tech selloff drives Nasdaq, MSCI global stocks index down
  • US 10-year Treasury yield falls 5.8 basis points to 4.931%
  • US crude settles at $104.12 a barrel; Brent at $117.63

By Sinéad Carew and Iain Withers

A sharp selloff in Wall Street's tech shares pushed MSCI's global index down 1.5% on Friday, sending investors to the safety of US bonds on fears that hefty cash-burning AI investments may not deliver sufficient returns.

Shares in chipmaker Intel < INTC.O> plunged 28.6% and Amazon shares lost 1.4% after their results each showed that they burned through cash while investing heavily in AI-related development. Intel also said PC demand had slowed, and that it could persist through next year.

Shares in Google parent Alphabet lost another 1.4%, having slid 12.6% on Thursday, after it reported that massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative.

"We've had such a huge move up in the whole complex," said Sahak Manuelian, managing director for global equities sales and trading at Wedbush Securities, referring to AI-related stocks. "When you've had the parabolic-like moves, it makes for a very nasty downdraft. I think that's what we're seeing. And then you have people that are starting to pull money out and going to other areas."

Earlier, Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera, described Friday's stock trading as a "horror show" with AI spending being the villain as cash burn and elevated capex prompted questions about whether the AI returns will "justify the outlays."

Goldman also said pressure from rising oil prices due to more attacks in the Middle East and concerns about a hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, added to the gloom. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies fell.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX fell 140.32 points, or 1.82%, to 7,580.07 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 747.73 points, or 2.86%, to 25,437.00.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe EURONEXT:IACWI fell 17.15 points, or 1.51%, to 1,115.47. Earlier, the pan-European STOXX 600 index finished down 0.36%.

On Wall Street, Intel's selloff spread across the chip sector. The PHLX semiconductor index finished down more than 7% after touching its lowest level since May, marking its biggest daily drop since late June. The S&P 500 technology index lost 4.2% in its weakest day since early June.

Investors looking for safer bets pushed up consumer staples and utilities . But the top performer on the day was energy , which was bolstered by oil's rally and results from Exxon Mobil and Chevron . The oil majors posted strong profits due to big refining margins driven by supply disruptions from Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and the Iran war.

In currencies, the yen was headed for its third consecutive daily gain against the dollar on Friday after the Bank of Japan held rates steady but revised up its inflation forecast, while a fresh wave of selling in AI shares triggered demand for non-dollar safe havens.

The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.04% to 101.92, with the euro down 0.13% at $1.1163.

Against the Japanese yen , the dollar weakened 0.1% to 157.54.

In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 2.49% to $76,877.30. Ethereum declined 1.01% to $2,236.76.

US Treasuries rose and the benchmark 10-year yield was eyeing its biggest monthly drop in nearly three years as the selloff in technology-related stocks pushed investors into the safe-haven asset.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 5.8 basis points to 4.931% while the 30-year bond (US30YT=RR) yield fell 1.97 basis points to 5.3093%.

The 2-year note (US2YT=RR) yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, fell 6.64 basis points to 4.59%.

Oil prices settled at six-month highs as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The war has lingered for eight months without a resolution. On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was attacked, highlighting the ongoing supply risks.

US crude settled up 2.08%, or $2.12, to $104.12 a barrel. Brent finished at $117.63 per barrel, up 2.4%, or $2.76 a barrel, on the day.

Precious metals fell. Gold dropped to a one-year low on Friday and silver slid below $50 an ounce for the first time since November 2025, as higher energy prices and persistent inflation concerns strengthened expectations that US interest rates will stay high.

Spot gold fell 3.63% to $3,874.58 an ounce and spot silver fell 6.36% to $49.06 an ounce.

data.title: Why gold plunged to its lowest price in a year despite renewed Iran jitters
data.description:
By Myra P. Saefong

Gold and stocks falling together is 'very reminiscent of 2008,' says analyst

Gold prices sank to their lowest price in over a year on Friday.

The plunge in safe-haven gold to its lowest price in a year on Friday seems to fly in the face of jitters around the potential for fresh turmoil in the Middle East following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

Investors, in the recent past, reliably flocked to the safety of gold, Treasurys and the U.S. dollar when regional conflict or war between nations looked imminent, or likely to intensify. But in President Donald Trump's second term, many of the traditional safe-haven moves have been turned on their head.

The tech-heavy gains driving the four-year bull run in U.S. stocks - and any sharp reversals - also now appear to be shaking things up following previous flight-to-safety playbooks.

A sharp selloff in equities through Friday has "created collateral damage in the precious-metals markets due to a liquidity-driven flight to safety," said Dana Samuelson, president of American Gold Exchange. In other words, investors hit by losses in the stock market were scrambling for cash, and found some by selling gold.

Gold prices settled Friday at $3,898.90 an ounce on Comex, with the most-active December contract (GCZ26) (GC00) down 3.3% for the session, according to Dow Jones Market Data. They tallied a loss of 10% for the month of October. That was the lowest settlement price since Oct. 2, 2025.

An equity selloff coincided with an already "weak and vulnerable" gold market that was hovering just above its major July support level of $3,975, said Samuelson. Once gold broke that support technical, that exacerbated its decline, he said.

Benchmark U.S. stock indexes traded broadly lower Friday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA ending 1.1% lower, the S&P 500 SPX tumbling 1.8% and the Nasdaq Composite Index COMP bearing the worst of it, with a 2.9% plunge.

"When equity markets drop hard, people look for liquidity," said Michael Armbruster, co-founder and managing partner at futures brokerage Altavest.

Markets across the board, however, seem to be "front-running growing concerns that there could be major and destabilizing military escalations in the Persian Gulf as early as next week," said American Gold Exchange's Samuelson.

Indeed, recent comments from Trump warrant concern. In a social-media post earlier this month, he ruled out U.S. military action against Iran ahead of the U.S. election on Nov. 3, but news reports indicate potential major strike plans have been drawn up.

Despite the high risks of escalation in the Middle East and a resumption of a regional war in the near future, gold has seen persistent pressure and it's had a difficult time sustaining a broader recovery, said Samer Hasn, senior market analyst at XS.com.

That's because a deteriorating situation in the region, along with resilience in the U.S. economy, may mean the Federal Reserve will keep a higher-for-longer interest-rate policy and keep Treasury yields elevated - preventing gold from recovering sustainably, he said in Friday commentary.

Meanwhile, "growth fears are the new news in the wake of in-line tech earnings and the selloff gaining some momentum across the AI sector," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management.

Should the selloff in AI intensify, especially if the election indicates opposition to data-center build-outs, gold may find some support, he said.

Longer term, Altavest's Armbruster suggested that gold prices could be headed higher, particularly if the Federal Reserve leans toward rate cuts in 2027.

The situation with gold and the stock market falling together is very reminiscent of 2008, he said. That year, gold bottomed by October and gold prices then climbed by more than 250% over the next three years, he said.

It is going to take a lot of money-printing to continue to finance the U.S. debt, Armbruster said. In the longer run, that is "extremely bullish for gold," he said, adding that Altavest has advised gold bugs "to keep their powder dry until year end."

"Do not buy this dip, yet," he said.

-Myra P. Saefong
